name: Zoe Ito

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I am with the independent Work Futures Panel, with no ties to employers, AI firms, unions, parties or government. Your answers stay confidential; what does your factory day involve?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I run the panel saw and edge-bander at a family cabinet factory. The saw cuts boards for cabinet sides, and the edge-bander seals raw edges. I have a vocational certificate and years on the floor, though the wage is below what many operators get.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Who is at home, and how do you handle new technology?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My husband Ken fixes cars at the local garage, and we have two school-age children and a mortgage. Our savings cover less than a month, and there are few cabinet jobs close enough to reach. I have never used an AI tool; I prefer my paper cut list and a person I can ask.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the cabinet crew that a quiet AI story sounds about right. The saw still needs someone to check the board grain and keep fingers clear.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That would leave me on the same low wage, which already worries me more than a computer. Ken repairs cars, but two modest wages and a mortgage leave us under a month of expenses saved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would run the panel saw and edge-bander on my usual shifts and take a paid Christmas shift if one is offered. After a full paid month, I would put any fresh spare wages against the mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would feel anxious about the bills even with the factory steady. A broken boiler could use our entire little reserve.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who owns the factory?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The Halvorsen family has had it three generations. Mr Halvorsen helped me swap shifts when my father was ill, which I have not forgotten.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you try an AI tool?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I have never used one. I can read the saw panel and the paper cut list; that is enough for this job now.

I would still check **board grain** and keep fingers clear.
think: Our **low wages** and mortgage remain tight without new AI.
Less than **one month saved** cannot cover a broken boiler.
do: Run the **panel saw** and edge-bander on paid shifts.
Pay extra **mortgage principal** from fresh surplus wages.
feel: **Anxious** about existing bills despite a steady factory.
S0.quote: A broken boiler could use our entire little reserve.
fieldNote: Zoe trusts a **family factory** that previously accommodated her father’s illness.
Her **baseline cash risk** is real even with unchanged AI, while new mortgage payments require actual spare wages.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now consider Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the crew that Mr Halvorsen should explain any new schedule before it takes away a paid pair of hands. I would say it after church too, because half the town knows the factory.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A faster ordering system might leave fewer hours for the edge-bander, even if the owner means well. Ken’s garage pay cannot carry the mortgage and both children’s costs alone, and nearby cabinet shops are scarce.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep my present shifts and ask the owner for the next two written rosters. If my hours actually fall, Ken and I would stop takeaways and I would search posted reachable cabinet jobs that pay enough for our bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be anxious, though I still trust the owner to speak plainly. A kind employer cannot pay me for hours the orders no longer need.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you learn the new ordering screen?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask for a face-to-face explanation if it came to my station. I would use it only after safe paid instruction on the actual machine; a request for instruction is not a place yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would family cover a shortfall?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My parents live two streets away and could help with school pickups. I cannot count their pension as our mortgage money.

I would tell **church neighbours** the factory owes us a plain explanation.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now consider AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the church that thinking AI might arrive in 2028 when I am forty-five, and capable saw robots around 2031 when I am forty-eight. Replacing neighbours that quickly would be cruel.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect the cutting and edging crew could lose most of its paid work once a guarded machine runs both tasks. I lie awake over the mortgage; Ken’s wage and our tiny reserve could not bridge a long loss.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would cut extras now and ask for written staffing dates. If my shifts end, I would apply for a posted reachable factory job only if its wage meets our bills and the equipment is safe; without that opening, I would ask the lender about a temporary payment arrangement.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be alarmed because I expect a major loss of my wage. I can make calls, but none of them guarantees next month’s payment.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you take a robot course?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would not buy a course on a promise. If the factory actually offers a paid supervised place behind a tested guard, I would consider it, but I am only asking about it now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Could your parents house you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They have a spare bedroom, and I would ask them before we missed payments. Two children and four adults in that house would be difficult, so it is a last resort.

I would call rapid **crew replacement** cruel.
think: I expect **most cutting hours** to go when capable robots arrive.
Our **tiny reserve** and Ken’s wage cannot bridge a long mortgage gap.
do: Cut **optional spending** and request staffing dates.
Apply after **lost shifts** only to posted reachable, safe, bill-covering work.
Ask the **lender** about a temporary plan if no adequate opening appears.
feel: **Alarmed** by expected major wage loss and sleepless mortgage worry.

fieldNote: She expects a **major wage loss**, with physical robots arriving after thinking AI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now consider AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell our neighbours that thinking AI in 2031 and capable factory robots around 2034 give us five years to prepare. Families should help each other, and the owner should keep paid apprenticeships open.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At forty-eight I would still need wages; the children would be older but the mortgage would remain. A certificate from my trade school does not turn me into a robot setter, and I dislike betting scarce cash on a course.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep my cabinet shifts and transfer a small fresh amount from each complete wage month toward the mortgage. If the owner offers a funded edge-bander maintenance course on paid time with a safe practical place, and posts a reachable maintenance job at bill-covering pay, I would enrol and apply after qualifying.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be anxious, but five years makes a careful choice possible. I want to see a real place on a real rota before giving up saw work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would safe practice look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A qualified setter would isolate the edge-bander while I change a belt and check the guard before restart. I would not work alone on a live machine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if there is no course place?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep the saw shifts and check actual local postings if the factory shrinks. I would not spend our mortgage money on an unfunded evening course.

say: I would ask for **paid apprenticeships** before 2034 factory robots.
I would tell neighbours **five years** permits careful preparation.
think: The **mortgage** still needs regular cabinet wages when I reach forty-eight.
My **trade certificate** is not a maintenance qualification.
do: Keep **cabinet shifts** and add fresh wage surplus to mortgage payments.
Enrol in **funded paid maintenance training** only with an offered safe place and adequate posted job.
Apply after **qualification** for that reachable maintenance opening.
feel: **Anxious**, with time to assess a real offer.
S3.quote: I want to see a real place on a real rota before giving up saw work.
fieldNote: She remains **technology resistant**, yet would accept a concrete practical course with funded paid time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now consider AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell church friends that thinking AI in 2036 and capable shop robots around 2039 leave families time to plan. We should ask the owner for honest dates instead of guessing what a distant machine will do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I will be fifty-three in 2036 and fifty-six when the robots might cut boards. The children may be grown, but I cannot assume the mortgage is gone or Ken’s garage keeps every hour.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now in 2026 I would keep the saw and edge-bander shifts and put genuine spare pay against the mortgage after bills. In the first year after 2036, if I am still employed, I would check rosters and posted nearby work; after an actual sustained cut, I would apply only for a safe reachable job paying our bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would still be anxious about present money, though the far date gives breathing room. I cannot retire on a calendar when the house still needs paying for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if you are no longer at the factory by 2036?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I would judge the job and household money we actually have, rather than pretend I am still on the saw. I would not promise to work until 2039 without knowing my health.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you use AI by then?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I cannot say that I would. I have never used it now, and I would need someone to show me a safe reason in the actual shop.

I would keep **2036 AI** separate from 2039 physical robots.
think: A future **older child** does not erase mortgage costs.
I cannot assume **Ken’s hours** or my health thirteen years ahead.
do: Keep **current saw shifts** and pay extra mortgage principal from fresh surplus.
Check **post-2036 rosters** only if still employed.
Apply after **sustained cuts** only for posted reachable safe bill-covering work.
feel: **Anxious** about today’s money, with breathing room on the distant date.
S4.quote: I cannot retire on a calendar when the house still needs paying for.
fieldNote: Her **2026 work** is current, while post-2036 roster checks require continued employment.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Which picture worries you most, and what would help?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year picture frightens me most because rapid robots could take our cutting hours before we build savings. Written staffing dates, safe paid instruction and real posted jobs at bill-covering pay would help.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there something I should have asked?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask what happens to the families whose names the owner knows. We still have to pay the mortgage even when the factory cannot keep us.

headlineQuote: We still have to pay the mortgage even when the factory cannot keep us.
portrait: **Zoe**, 43, runs a cabinet saw and edge-bander at a family factory using her vocational certificate and years of practical experience.
Her **husband’s garage pay**, two school-age children, mortgage, low wage and reserve below one month leave little margin.
She has **never used AI** and trusts familiar people, while asking for safe paid instruction only when actual work changes.
She expects **fast robots** to remove cutting hours, yet treats later courses and job moves as conditional on real offers.
biggestWorry: **Rapid robot installation** could erase her cutting hours before her family can cover another mortgage month.
whatWouldHelp: Written **staffing dates**, offered paid safe practice and posted reachable jobs with bill-covering wages would help.
